title: SQL NULL Functions: COALESCE, IFNULL and NULLIF
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL NULL Functions: COALESCE, IFNULL and NULLIF.
Write SQLite-compatible SQL for the topic or a clearly labelled equivalent.
Predict result rows using the lesson's sample data.
Identify dialect limitations, NULL behaviour and common errors.
Apply the topic to a practical data task.

understand.concept: NULL-handling functions let queries substitute a fallback for missing values or turn a selected value into NULL. COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument; SQLite IFNULL takes two arguments; NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments compare equal. Similar functions have different names and details across DBMS products.
understand.whyItMatters: Explicit NULL handling makes reports, calculations and comparisons predictable when data is incomplete or when zero/empty values need special treatment.
understand.analogy: Think of a SQL query as a carefully specified instruction for selecting or shaping rows in a database.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL evaluation order, transaction guarantees, NULL logic or DBMS-specific implementation details.

explain.narrative:
## Core functions
- COALESCE(a,b,c) returns the first non-NULL argument and is supported by SQLite and major DBMS products.
- IFNULL(a,b) is SQLite's two-argument form; MySQL also has IFNULL. SQL Server uses ISNULL with different type rules; Oracle commonly uses NVL.
- NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when a equals b; otherwise it returns a.

Do not confuse NULL with 0 or an empty string. Arithmetic involving NULL normally produces NULL. Use these functions deliberately and check result types in the target DBMS. W3Schools' SQL NULL Functions topic includes multiple product-specific forms.

## Common mistakes
- Assuming syntax is identical across all database engines.
- Omitting explicit column lists when moving data.
- Ignoring NULL, constraints or result ordering.
- Treating a documented dialect example as executable SQLite syntax.

## Best practices
Use explicit columns, test against the target DBMS/version, keep setup scripts repeatable, and verify results with SELECT queries.

examples.title: Use COALESCE to show a fallback
examples.expectedOutput: Asha | Rajahmundry; Bilal | City not provided; Chitra | Vijayawada
examples.explanation: COALESCE returns the first argument that is not NULL.

examples.title: Use IFNULL for a two-choice fallback
examples.explanation: SQLite IFNULL accepts exactly two arguments and returns the fallback when the first is NULL.

examples.title: Use NULLIF to avoid division by zero
examples.explanation: NULLIF(target,0) returns NULL for a zero denominator, avoiding a divide-by-zero calculation.

examples.title: Choose the first available contact field
examples.explanation: COALESCE checks arguments from left to right and returns the first available contact.

examples.title: Keep NULL distinct from a real zero
examples.expectedOutput: 1 | Recorded zero; 2 | Not recorded; 3 | Recorded value
examples.explanation: NULLIF and COALESCE should not erase the meaningful difference between a recorded zero and missing data.

options: The last argument regardless of NULL
questions.explanation: COALESCE scans arguments from left to right and returns the first non-NULL value.

questions.prompt: How many arguments does SQLite IFNULL accept?
questions.explanation: SQLite IFNULL(X,Y) is a two-argument NULL fallback function.

options: When a and b compare equal
Whenever b is greater than a
Only when both values are text
questions.answer: When a and b compare equal
questions.explanation: NULLIF returns NULL when its two arguments are equal.

questions.prompt: Why use NULLIF(target,0) as a denominator?
options: It converts a zero denominator to NULL and avoids a divide-by-zero calculation
It converts every nonzero denominator to zero
It deletes rows with zero targets
It rounds the result to an integer
questions.answer: It converts a zero denominator to NULL and avoids a divide-by-zero calculation
questions.explanation: NULLIF returns NULL for a zero target, so the division result is NULL.

questions.prompt: How should a query test whether a column is missing?
questions.explanation: SQL NULL comparisons use three-valued logic; IS NULL is the correct test.
